---
title: "learning curves"
---

## what a learning curve shows

- a learning curve plots training and validation error (or score) against the amount of training data used, from a small fraction up to the full training set
- it answers a different question from a loss-vs-iteration curve: not "is training converging?" but "would more data help this model?"
- each point is typically generated by training on a random subset of a given size (often averaged across several random subsets) and evaluating on both that subset and a fixed validation set

## reading the curve

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| pattern | training error | validation error | gap | diagnosis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| underfitting / high bias | high, flattens early | high, close to training error | small | model too simple — more data won't help much; try a more flexible model or better features |
| overfitting / high variance | low | substantially higher than training | large, narrows slowly | model too flexible for the data available — more data likely helps, or regularise/simplify |
| good fit | low | similar to training, both still improving slightly with more data | small | reasonable fit; more data may still help a little |

:::

- as training-set size grows, training error usually rises slightly (harder to fit more points perfectly) while validation error falls — the two curves converging toward each other and flattening suggests more data has diminishing returns
- if both curves are still falling steeply at the right edge of the plot, more data is likely to keep helping; if they've flattened, the bottleneck is the model or features, not data volume

## learning curves vs validation curves

- a **learning curve** varies the amount of training data, with the model/hyperparameters held fixed — it diagnoses whether to get more data
- a **validation curve** (e.g. error vs. $\lambda$ in [regularisation](regularisation.qmd#choosing-lambda--reading-the-graphs), or vs. tree depth, or vs. $k$) varies a hyperparameter, with the training-set size held fixed — it diagnoses which hyperparameter setting generalises best
- both compare training against validation/held-out performance; the x-axis is the key difference between them

## practical considerations

- learning curves are a cheap way to decide whether collecting more data is worth it before investing in a larger dataset
- compute them using the training set only, with an internal split or cross-validation for the "validation" error at each size — the test set stays untouched
- for small or imbalanced datasets, average over several random subsets at each size, since a single subset can give a noisy estimate
- a wide, non-shrinking gap between training and validation error — even as data grows — points toward overfitting that more data alone won't fix; regularisation or a simpler model is the more direct remedy, see [residuals & the bias–variance tradeoff](bias-variance.qmd)
